A sack is a large, flexible bag — typically made of rough, sturdy material like cloth, burlap (jute fabric), or heavy paper — used to hold and carry bulk goods. It is wider and larger than a regular bag, open at the top, and can usually be tied or sealed shut.

Think of the kind of large, simple bag you might see filled with grain, flour, potatoes, sand, or coal. That is a sack.

"The farmer loaded three sacks of wheat onto the cart."
"They stacked sandbags — sacks filled with sand — along the riverbank to stop the flood."
Meaning 1: A Large Bag (Physical Object)

This is the word's most fundamental meaning. A sack is a big, rough-textured bag made to hold heavy or bulky things in large quantities. Unlike a delicate shopping bag or a refined purse, a sack is purely functional — it is designed for strength and capacity, not elegance.

Common things stored or transported in sacks: rice, potatoes, coffee beans, flour, coal, cement, fertiliser, animal feed.

"She bought a sack of onions from the market."
"The construction workers emptied sack after sack of concrete into the mixer."
Meaning 2: The Amount a Sack Holds

By natural extension, "a sack of something" also refers to the quantity of whatever fills it, not just the bag itself. So if someone says "buy me a sack of sugar," they mean the full amount that comes packaged in one sack.

"We went through two sacks of rice this month."
Meaning 3: The Sack — Losing Your Job

In British and Australian English especially, "the sack" is a well-known informal way of referring to being fired or dismissed from a job. This always appears with the definite article the.

You'll see it in a few fixed phrases:

  • "to get the sack" = to be fired
  • "to give someone the sack" = to fire someone
  • "to face the sack" = to risk being fired

"He kept arriving late to work, so the manager finally gave him the sack."
"She was afraid she'd get the sack if her boss found out she'd made the error."

This meaning is used in everyday conversation and in newspapers in Britain, Australia, and other parts of the English-speaking world. In American English, people are more likely to say "fired" or "laid off," but "the sack" is still widely understood.
Meaning 4: Bed (Informal/Slang)

In informal, especially American, English, "the sack" can mean bed. This shows up most commonly in a pair of well-known idioms:

  • "hit the sack" = to go to bed, to go to sleep
  • "in the sack" = in bed (sleeping, or sometimes used to suggest intimacy)

"I'm completely exhausted — I'm going to hit the sack."
"He was already in the sack by nine o'clock."

The image here is of an old-fashioned sleeping sack or bedroll, something you literally crawl into.
Meaning 5: In American Football — Tackling the Quarterback

In the sport of American football (and in discussions about it), a sack is a specific type of play: it happens when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage — meaning before the quarterback has had a chance to throw the ball forward.

A sack is considered a big, positive event for the defence, because it pushes the attacking team further back and disrupts their game.

"The defensive end recorded his fifth sack of the season."
"The quarterback was under constant pressure and suffered two sacks in the final quarter."

The word functions both as a singular event ("a sack") and as something that can be counted ("three sacks").
Meaning 6: The Violent Plundering of a City (Historical)

In historical and literary writing, "the sack" of a city or place refers to the thorough looting, destruction, and ransacking of that place by an invading or conquering force — typically after a battle or siege. It describes a scene of violence, theft, and devastation carried out systematically by soldiers after they've taken over.

"The sack of Rome in 410 AD shocked the entire ancient world."
"History books describe the sack of the city as a three-day orgy of destruction and theft."

You will encounter this meaning in history books, documentaries, and literature. It always carries a sense of large-scale, brutal destruction.
Meaning 7: A Loose, Shapeless Garment (Fashion)

In fashion and clothing, a sack (sometimes called a sack dress or sack coat) refers to a loose, straight, and relatively shapeless garment — one that hangs from the shoulders without following the curves of the body. The name comes from the resemblance to a simple bag draped over the body.

"She wore a simple cotton sack dress on the warm afternoon."
"The sack silhouette was fashionable in the 1950s and 1960s."

This meaning is fairly specific to discussions of fashion, costume history, and clothing design.
Meaning 8: A Type of Wine (Archaic/Historical)

In older English literature and historical texts, sack was the name given to a dry white wine imported from Spain and the Canary Islands — similar to what we today call sherry. This meaning is archaic, meaning it is no longer in active everyday use, but you will come across it if you read older literature (particularly from the 16th–18th centuries, including Shakespeare).

"He called for a cup of sack to warm himself."

If you see "sack" used as a drink in an older text, this is what it means.
Quick Orientation: How to Know Which Meaning Is Meant

Since "sack" has many meanings, context almost always makes it clear:

  • A sack of something → a large bag containing goods
  • Got the sack / gave someone the sack → fired from a job
  • Hit the sack / in the sack → bed or sleep
  • Recorded a sack (in a sports report) → football tackle
  • The sack of [a place name] → historical looting and destruction
  • Sack dress / sack coat → loose, shapeless clothing
  • A cup of sack (in old literature) → wine
Summary

MeaningRegisterCommon regions

To put it all in one picture: sack starts as something simple and physical — a large rough bag — and from there it spreads out into the language in many directions: the bag you lose your job "into," the bag you sleep "in," the forceful tackle, the brutal conquest, the shapeless dress, and the old wine. Every use carries, in some way, the same underlying feeling: something large, rough, and plain.
